A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we introduce the task, we show how it can be done using existing corpora and existing methods, and then we show how it could be useful in summarization.

we introduce the task to automatically identify general and specific sentences, we explore the use of discourse information for this task and we use the identified sentences to analyze the distribution in human and machine generated summaries of news articles, and we show that the distribution of general sentences in machine summaries is different than human summaries.

we are interested in understanding how the structure of news articles and news summaries is affected by the type of sentences they contain, and whether the type of sentences is a useful feature for summarization.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the task of identifying specific sentences can be used to analyze the quality of news summaries, both human and machine, and to identify a new task for summarization, namely, generation of general sentences, which we believe is important for abstractive summaries.

the task of identifying the specificity of sentences can be useful to the summarization community, and that it may be feasible to train a classifier using discourse information from existing large corpora.
the distribution of general versus specific sentences is a good measure for assessing the quality of a summary.
